frontMatter.title: The Criteria: Every Mechanism, Its Harm, and Its Points
frontMatter.description: What each of the 99 mechanisms means, why it helps or hurts, how harmful it is, and why it removes the points it removes — the reference behind every score in the 111-language comparison.

frontMatterLines: title: "The Criteria: Every Mechanism, Its Harm, and Its Points"

description: What each of the 99 mechanisms means, why it helps or hurts, how harmful it is, and why it removes the points it removes — the reference behind every score in the 111-language comparison.

blocks.q: **Companion to:** [The Great Language Smackdown](index.qmd) · [the Scoreboard and the full per-language data](scoreboard.qmd) · [the scoring model](objective-coupling-scoring-model.qmd)

blocks.p: Every language on this site is measured against **one inventory of 99 mechanisms** — the same list, with the same weights, and the same arithmetic, for all 111. The inventory has three parts: **Core coupling** (46 mechanisms, 350 points), **Ecosystem coupling** (34 mechanisms, 256 points), and **Engineering readiness** (19 mechanisms, 171 points). No language gets a private criterion, and no mechanism is applied to one language and then set aside for another. That is what makes the comparison a comparison: a difference between two scores is a difference in which mechanisms are present, never a difference in how strictly the two languages were judged.

This page explains each criterion. For every mechanism it gives what the mechanism is, the kind of coupling it imposes and why, how harmful it is — the weight tier that removes the points — and a concrete example. The [Scoreboard](scoreboard.qmd) publishes the other half: which mechanisms each language has, and the score that follows. The [scoring model](objective-coupling-scoring-model.qmd) gives the arithmetic and the tests that decide presence.

**Read every entry as a harm.** The inventory of 99 mechanisms contains no features, no positives, and no offsets. A mechanism is in the list because a maintainer pays for it when the mechanism is present, and a language's score is what remains once the present share is subtracted from that axis inventory. One mechanism, `V5`, carries the `Recorded` severity: it states a fact and removes no points. The same practice appears on the pages that record a boundary no current document decides: Turbo Pascal and SAS, where a delivery row marked *recorded, not priced* states a crossing release boundary, and PHP, where a data row marks the format the manual names without a version field or a cross-release rule — a format the probe harness has round-tripped across the 8.0 to 8.4 release pairs without reproducing a break, which tests the format and still promises nothing.

Two parts of a program are **coupled** where they must agree about one shared thing: a type, a heap, a lock, a name space, a platform ABI, a runtime. The agreement is the cost. It has to be established when the code is written, it has to be maintained while the code lives, and it has to be re-established whenever either side changes.
A language mechanism is a **coupling criterion** when it forces agreement that the programmer cannot refuse. Three properties decide how much that costs:

rawtable: | Property | Question | Effect on the weight |
| **Breadth** | How much of the program has to agree — one call site, one module, or the whole program? | A wider agreement costs more |
| **Escape** | Can a programmer opt out of the mechanism locally? | No escape costs more |
| **Silence** | Does the language say so, or must a reader discover it? | A silent obligation costs more |

blocks.p: A mechanism that makes the whole program agree, with no local way out, and nothing in the language that records the agreement, is **High**. A mechanism that forces agreement across ordinary code, escapable only by a convention that the whole codebase must keep, is **Moderate**. A mechanism whose agreement is confined to a boundary, and removable by a contained workaround, is **Minor**.
That is the whole rationale for the weights. The tier is a judgment about **breadth, escape, and silence** — not a count of incidents, and not a substitute for measurement.

**Every entry names its coupling.** After the tier, each entry states the kind of coupling the mechanism imposes and why it cannot be refused: which two parties must agree, what they must agree about, and which property of the language forces the agreement. The kind is the name of the shared resource — a type, a call target, a heap, a schedule, a version, a supply — so the entries read as a catalogue of shared resources rather than as a list of complaints.

rawtable: | Tier | Weight | What the tier asserts | Cost on Core when it is alone |
| **High** | −15 | Agreement across the whole program, no local escape, and nothing in the language that records it | −4.6 |
| **Moderate** | −8 | Agreement across ordinary code, escapable only by a whole-codebase convention | −2.5 |
| **Minor** | −4 | Agreement confined to a boundary, removable by a contained workaround | −1.2 |
| **Recorded** | 0 | The event is a fact the reader must know, and its direction is not mechanically determinable | 0 — it never enters a sum |

blocks.p: **The fourth tier is not a weight.** A price has one direction: the same presence must always mean the same cost. Where the direction is not fixed, no single number can state the cost. A mechanism whose sign varies cannot enter the sum without making that sum incomparable across languages and across releases — the same mark would have to mean a gain and a loss at once, so two scores would no longer be arithmetically comparable, and two analysts would no longer reach the same number. The model therefore **records** such a mechanism: the mark is present or absent, the observation beside it states what changed, why, and how a deployment reverses it, and the score is untouched. `V5` is the only mechanism in this tier.

Within one dimension the present weights are **summed**, and each mechanism contributes its share of the axis inventory: a mechanism of weight `w` costs `100 × w ÷ inventory weight` score points, and the dimension cost is the sum over its present mechanisms. There is no cap and no curve. The share is a rubric choice, not a measurement: it stays additive because a maintainer pays every forced coupling, it stays bounded because the numerator can never exceed the inventory, and it is monotone, so removing a mechanism always moves the number. The inventory weight states what the model knows about the axis, not a ceiling on what the axis can cost.

Each entry gives the mechanism's code and tier, what the mechanism **is**, the **kind of coupling** it imposes and why, an **example**, and — where the criterion is easy to misread — what its presence does **not** mean.

Presence is a factual question about the **language**: does the language hand the programmer this construct? It is not a judgment about the code. Every language permits a global; `C1` asks whether a global is the *default* home for state.

**Who imposes the mechanism.** Every entry carries one tag: *Imposed by: language*, *runtime*, or *context*. A **language** mechanism is decided by the compiler — the construct is in the source, and the compiler accepts or rejects it. A **runtime** mechanism is decided by the executor: the memory manager, the compiler that runs later, the thread scheduler, or a default the platform chooses. A **context** mechanism is decided by the surroundings: the vendor, the toolchain, the market, the documentation, or the standard. The tag is meta-information and never changes a weight. It tells a reader where a remedy would have to happen: in the code, in the deployment, or outside both.

**A check behind a project switch.** Some mechanisms depend on a compiler switch. The mark uses the configuration the language's own project initialiser writes for the version shown, because that is what a new project gets without a decision. `tsc --init` writes `"strict": true` (which sets `strictNullChecks`), so TypeScript is not charged `T10`; `dotnet new` writes `<Nullable>enable</Nullable>`, so C# is not charged `T10`; Visual Basic's compiler default is `Option Strict Off` and the SDK template sets no `OptionStrict`, so the narrowing conversion is charged `T2`. Where the initialiser writes no switch, the compiler default governs. A check that only a separate tool supplies is never counted — that is what `T1` already says about `mypy` in CI.

**A mitigation is not an absence.** Some languages offer an opt-in construct that avoids a mechanism — `@CompileStatic` in Groovy, `try-with-resources` in Java, `reified` in Kotlin, a lint rule, or a flag the initialiser does not set. The mechanism stays charged, because the default code still pays it and avoiding it needs knowledge the language does not force. The model measures what the *language* imposes, not what a disciplined team can achieve. If a mitigation lowered the score, two teams on the same language would score differently, and the language would have no score. The mitigation is recorded on the language page as a strength or a trade-off, never as a discount. The line between a mitigation and an absence is the project-switch rule above.

The readiness axis uses the same three tiers and the same severity-share arithmetic as coupling. It asks a different question: not how much the language forces two parts of a program to agree, but whether the artifact can be rebuilt, verified, observed, worked in quickly, connected to another language, and governed openly. Breadth, escape, and silence decide the tier here too.
Present weights are summed, divided by the axis inventory weight (350 on Core), and the score is 100 minus that share. Here is Go's Core score, from the criteria above:

Memory carries 20 raw points and Concurrency 20, so each costs 100 × 20 ÷ 350 = 5.7 of the 100. The [Scoreboard](scoreboard.qmd) holds the same data for all 111 languages and reproduces every score the same way.

blocks.text: What the criteria do not measure

blocks.p: The inventory prices the **language**, before any design decision, and it is honest about its limits.

ul: **Not design quality.** Two programs in the same language differ more from each other than the languages differ from one another. A program can cluster what the language scatters, and a good design decision is exactly that act. The score is the raw material, not the outcome.

**Not team skill or process.** A discipline that a team keeps — a checked build, a mandatory code review of ownership, a lint rule — can hold a High mechanism at bay in practice. The model charges it anyway, because the discipline is not in the language and cannot be relied on by the next team.

**Not severity in a particular system.** The weight judges breadth, escape, and silence. A Minor mechanism in a hot path can cost more than a High one in a corner of the program, and the model deliberately does not try to price that. A weight is a property of the mechanism; a cost is a property of a system.

**Not the last word on any one language.** Every mechanism mark is a factual claim about the language, and a factual claim can be wrong. When one is, the mark is corrected, and every score, table, and ranking derived from it is regenerated. The [Scoreboard](scoreboard.qmd) carries the data so that the claim can be checked rather than trusted.
